title: The Doctor & Pharmacy
description: Describing your symptoms at a clinic or pharmacy (apotek), understanding how to take the medicine, and asking the questions you'll want answered.

phrases.english: I've had a fever since yesterday.
phrases.registerNotes: Sejak, 'since', goes before the time: sejak tadi malam (since last night), sejak hari Senin.
phrases.pitfallNote: There's no 'have had' tense to build: the time word does the work, and demam stays as it is.

phrases.english: I've got a cough and a runny nose.
phrases.registerNotes: Pilek is a head cold, mainly the runny or blocked nose. People also say flu for an ordinary cold.

phrases.english: I've caught a chill. I feel run-down.
phrases.registerNotes: Everyone understands it, but at a clinic list the actual symptoms too.
phrases.cultureNote: Masuk angin, 'wind has got in', is the folk name for feeling achy, cold, bloated or off. A common home remedy is kerokan: scraping the back with a coin and oil, which leaves red stripes.

phrases.english: I've got a stomach ache and diarrhoea.
phrases.registerNotes: Sakit perut covers any tummy pain. Diare is the word to use with a doctor; you'll also hear the cruder mencret.

phrases.english: My head's spinning. I feel dizzy.
phrases.registerNotes: Kepala saya pusing is how you tell a doctor or a pharmacist; with friends, Pusing on its own.
phrases.pitfallNote: Pusing is a woozy, aching head, somewhere between dizzy and a headache; for a plain headache, sakit kepala is more exact. Pusing also means stressed: pusing soal uang.

phrases.english: What seems to be the problem?
phrases.registerNotes: What a doctor or nurse asks first. Keluhan is a complaint, the medical word for what's wrong with you; answer with your symptoms.
The answer to Sejak kapan? (Since when?) or Sudah berapa lama? (How long?). Dok, short for dokter, is how you address a doctor.

phrases.indonesian: Obatnya diminum tiga kali sehari, sesudah makan.
phrases.english: Take the medicine three times a day, after meals.
phrases.registerNotes: What the doctor or pharmacist tells you. Labels often write it 3 x 1: three times a day, one each time.
phrases.pitfallNote: You minum (drink) medicine in Indonesian, even tablets: Sudah minum obat?

phrases.english: Do I take it before or after meals?
phrases.registerNotes: The di- form keeps the medicine as the subject, which is how dosage talk works: Diminum berapa kali sehari? (How many times a day?)

phrases.english: Do I need a prescription for this?
phrases.registerNotes: Resep is a prescription, and also a recipe.
phrases.cultureNote: Pharmacies (apotek) sell many medicines over the counter, and the pharmacist will often suggest one; antibiotics officially need a prescription.

phrases.registerNotes: Alergi goes straight before the thing, with no word for 'to': alergi obat, alergi udang. Say it before anything is prescribed.
Apa at the start just marks a yes-or-no question in speech; apakah is the written form. Friends ask Parah, nggak? (Is it bad?)

phrases.indonesian: Bisa minta surat keterangan sakit, Dok?
phrases.english: Could I have a medical certificate, doctor?
phrases.registerNotes: For work or school. People call it surat sakit for short, and clinics are used to being asked.

phrases.english: Do I need to come back for a check-up?
phrases.registerNotes: Ask it as the doctor finishes. Dok is short for Dokter, the usual way to address a doctor.
phrases.pitfallNote: Kontrol is a follow-up visit, not 'control': Kontrol minggu depan, ya (Come back next week).
